OpenAI has just detailed how it will comply with the EU AI Act, which requires providers of generative AI systems to add recognisable markers to AI-generated text. Here's what you need to know.

Some background

A few months ago, Anthropic sparked controversy by saying that to comply with the EU AI Act, Claude would add watermarks to text through fine-tuned word choices.

Basically, Claude would occasionally pick one of several equally suitable words based on a hidden pattern, which Anthropic claimed has no real impact on the semantics, quality or readability of the response.

Anthropic also built a detection tool that can identify the pattern in a piece of text, thereby determining that the text was very likely written by Claude.

)

At the height of the controversy, Anthropic stressed that Claude was not going it alone, saying several other major AI providers were also implementing marking systems to comply with EU regulations.

OpenAI unveiled its approach today, which while similar in method, is far more limited in scope and applicability.

OpenAI's text watermarking system

According to OpenAI, "starting today, global API users can opt in to enabling text watermarking for specific models," and the company will "add invisible watermarks to eligible ChatGPT and Codex text outputs in the EU over the coming weeks."

So on the API side, text watermarking remains an opt-in feature for now; for ChatGPT and Codex, it will initially only be enabled for eligible users in the EU.

OpenAI is also opening up applications for its text watermark detection tool, initially limited to approved researchers and professional institutions, so the company can evaluate and improve the technology.

In terms of accuracy, OpenAI explicitly noted that the detection function still has obvious limitations, such as false negatives and false positives, with the problem being more obvious on shorter text or content in specific fields, "such as mathematics, where word choice is more constrained."

Here's how OpenAI describes textGrain (its text watermarking technology):

The company also noted that watermarks are harder to detect in shorter passages, and that editing modifications will significantly weaken the watermark's effectiveness:

Interestingly, when the company compared watermarked and unwatermarked text, the watermarked outputs scored slightly higher on several benchmarks, though the company believes there is no significant difference in overall performance.

Benchmark Unwatermarked text (Astra, max) Watermarked text (Astra, max) Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index 49.57 points 49.76 points AutomationBench 34.09% 34.86% DeepSWE v1.1 72.80% 71.68% Terminal-Bench 4.0 53.90% 56.06% Terminal-Bench Science 0.1 56.90% 60.00% BrowseComp 87.92% 87.35% HealthBench Professional 64.27% 64.60% GPQA Diamond 94.44% 93.94%

OpenAI also stressed that beyond the issues of false negatives and false positives, watermarks "cannot measure the degree of human involvement," "cannot establish ownership or responsibility," "cannot identify the user's identity," and also "cannot verify accuracy."

OpenAI added that "detecting no watermark does not mean the text was written by a human."

Finally, the company said it expects to revisit its approach as technology, standards and evidence evolve, while continuing to research how watermarks persist after editing and translation, and whether AI-assisted and AI-original content can be more effectively distinguished.
